Let $n\ge1$, let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable at
$x\in\mathbb R^n$, and put $g:=\nabla f(x)$ using the gradient convention of
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. Let $B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be a
symmetric matrix and let $\Delta>0$. A quadratic model at $x$ is

$$m(p):=f(x)+\langle g,p\rangle+\tfrac12 p^TBp,\qquad p\in\mathbb R^n,$$

with the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]
and matrix products as in [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. The
trust-region ball is $\mathcal B_\Delta:=\{p:\|p\|_2\le\Delta\}$. The
predicted reduction of a feasible step $p\in\mathcal B_\Delta$ is
$\operatorname{pred}(p):=m(0)-m(p)$. Its actual reduction is
$\operatorname{ared}(p):=f(x)-f(x+p)$. When $\operatorname{pred}(p)>0$, the
actual-to-predicted reduction ratio is

$$\rho(p):=\frac{\operatorname{ared}(p)}{\operatorname{pred}(p)}.$$

The quantity $\|B\|_2$ means the matrix norm induced by the Euclidean vector
norm, namely the $p=2$ case of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]]. It is not required
that $B=\nabla^2f(x)$ in this definition; exact Hessians and symmetric model
approximations are both admitted. The ratio is undefined when predicted
reduction is nonpositive, so an algorithm must use a separately justified
fallback or return a failure status in that case.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

For a real $m\times m$ matrix $H$, write $q_H(h):=\langle Hh,h\rangle$ using [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. It is **positive definite** when $q_H(h)>0$ for every $h\ne0$, **negative definite** when $q_H(h)<0$ for every $h\ne0$, **positive semidefinite** when $q_H(h)\ge0$ for every $h$, **negative semidefinite** when $q_H(h)\le0$ for every $h$, and **indefinite** when it takes both positive and negative values. For a twice differentiable scalar field, its Hessian matrix is the matrix of [[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]].

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a \le b$, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on the closed bounded interval $[a,b]$ ([[def-interval]],
[[def-continuity-real]]), and let $y \in \mathbb{R}$ satisfy

$$f(a) \le y \le f(b) \qquad \text{or} \qquad f(b) \le y \le f(a) .$$

Then there is $c \in [a,b]$ with $f(c) = y$.

**The construction is canonical, so no choice principle is used.** The bisection
below tests the left half first and takes the right half only when the left one
has been ruled out, so the passage from one interval to the next is a *function*
of that interval, and [[thm-recursion]] applies with nothing selected. This is
the same discipline the library uses wherever a sequence is built one term at a
time.

**Completeness of $\mathbb{R}$ is what does the work.** The bisection produces a
nested sequence of closed bounded intervals whose lengths tend to $0$, and it is
[[thm-nested-interval-property]] — hence the least-upper-bound property — that
supplies the point. Over an ordered field that is not complete the theorem
fails; the witness for that, stated for an arbitrary ordered field and worked
over $\mathbb{Q}$, is
[[cex-evt-and-ivt-fail-over-a-non-complete-field]], which states its own
$\varepsilon$-$\delta$ continuity inline and is not an instance of this page's
definition.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$, let
$\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$. Suppose $f$ and $g$ are continuous at
$c$ ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then:

1. $f + g$, $\alpha f$ and $fg$ are continuous at $c$;
2. $|f|$, the function $x \mapsto |f(x)|$, is continuous at $c$;
3. $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, defined pointwise by
   $x \mapsto \max\{f(x), g(x)\}$ and $x \mapsto \min\{f(x), g(x)\}$
   ([[def-max-min]]), are continuous at $c$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is continuous at
   $c$ as a function on $A_0$.

Moreover, with no hypothesis at all:

5. every constant function $A \to \mathbb{R}$ and the identity
   $\mathrm{id} : A \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto x$, are continuous on $A$; hence
   so is $x \mapsto x^{n}$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$
   ([[def-integer-power]]), and hence so is every **polynomial function**
   $x \mapsto a_0 + a_1 x + \dots + a_n x^{n}$ with real coefficients.

Consequently, if $f$ and $g$ are continuous **on** $A$ then so are $f+g$,
$\alpha f$, $fg$, $|f|$, $\max\{f,g\}$ and $\min\{f,g\}$, and
$(f/g)|_{A_0}$ is continuous on $A_0$.

**Claim 4 is stated on $A_0$ because $f/g$ is not defined where $g$ vanishes**,
and $g$ may well vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$. The hypothesis is
$g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ nowhere zero"; what it buys is that $c$ itself lies in
the smaller domain, which is what makes continuity there mean anything.

**Nothing here is proved through a sequence.** Claims 1 and 4 are read off from
[[thm-algebra-of-function-limits]], which is itself proved from $\varepsilon$
and $\delta$, and claims 2, 3 and 5 are proved directly below. So no choice
principle is used anywhere in this item.

derivations.claim:
By [F2], choose an orthogonal matrix $U$ such that
$D:=U^TBU=\operatorname{diag}(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n)$ with
$\mu_1\le\cdots\le\mu_n$. Put $c:=U^Tg$ and write $p=Uy$. Then
$q(Uy)=\sum_i(c_i y_i+\tfrac12\mu_i y_i^2)$ and
$\|Uy\|_2=\|y\|_2$, so it suffices to construct a minimizer in these
coordinates.

Set $\lambda_0:=\max(0,-\mu_1)$ and, for $\lambda>\lambda_0$,
define $\varphi(\lambda):=\sum_i c_i^2/(\mu_i+\lambda)^2$ and
$y_i(\lambda):=-c_i/(\mu_i+\lambda)$. Every denominator is positive, so
[F5] gives continuity of $\varphi$. Let
$Z:=\{i:\mu_i+\lambda_0=0\}$. If some $i\in Z$ has $c_i\ne0$, choose
$\lambda_a>\lambda_0$ with $\lambda_a-\lambda_0<|c_i|/\Delta$; its single
term gives $\varphi(\lambda_a)>\Delta^2$. Otherwise $c_i=0$ for $i\in Z$.
Then
$$\varphi_0:=\sum_{i\notin Z}\frac{c_i^2}{(\mu_i+\lambda_0)^2}$$
is finite. If $\varphi_0>\Delta^2$, each term with $i\notin Z$ is
continuous at $\lambda_0$ by [F5], while each term with $i\in Z$ is zero
for $\lambda>\lambda_0$ and extends as the constant zero. Thus the extension
with value $\varphi_0$ is continuous at $\lambda_0$, so choose
$\lambda_a>\lambda_0$ close enough that $\varphi(\lambda_a)>\Delta^2$.
In either case with $\varphi(\lambda_a)>\Delta^2$, put
$S:=\sum_i|\mu_i|$ and choose
$R>\max\{\lambda_a,S+2\|c\|_2/\Delta\}$. Then
$\mu_i+R>2\|c\|_2/\Delta$ for every $i$, giving
$\varphi(R)<\Delta^2/4<\Delta^2$. By [F4] on $[\lambda_a,R]$, choose
$\lambda>\lambda_0$ with $\varphi(\lambda)=\Delta^2$. The vector
$y_i=-c_i/(\mu_i+\lambda)$ then has norm $\Delta$,
$(D+\lambda I)y=-c$, and $D+\lambda I$ is positive definite.

In the remaining case every $i\in Z$ has $c_i=0$ and the finite sum
$\varphi_0$ in step 1.2 satisfies $\varphi_0\le\Delta^2$. Set
$y_i^0=-c_i/(\mu_i+\lambda_0)$ for $i\notin Z$ and $y_i^0=0$ for $i\in Z$.
If $\lambda_0=0$, take $y=y^0$; then
$D$ is positive semidefinite, $Dy=-c$, and $\|y\|_2\le\Delta$. If
$\lambda_0>0$, the zero-denominator coordinates form the least-eigenvalue
eigenspace. Add a vector $z$ supported on those coordinates with
$\|z\|_2^2=\Delta^2-\|y^0\|_2^2$ and take $y=y^0+z$. Such a vector exists
by scaling a unit eigenvector; it is orthogonal to $y^0$. Then
$(D+\lambda_0 I)y=-c$, $D+\lambda_0 I\succeq0$, and $\|y\|_2=\Delta$.
This is the hard-case construction.

In either construction, returning to $p=Uy$ gives a feasible vector and
a $\lambda\ge0$ with $(B+\lambda I)p=-g$, $B+\lambda I\succeq0$, and
$\lambda(\Delta-\|p\|_2)=0$. For every feasible $v$, direct expansion gives
$$q(v)-q(p)=\tfrac12(v-p)^T(B+\lambda I)(v-p)
+\tfrac\lambda2(\|p\|_2^2-\|v\|_2^2)\ge0,$$
because the first term is nonnegative by [F3] and the second is zero if
$\lambda=0$ and nonnegative otherwise. Thus the constructed vector is a global
minimizer.

Conversely, let $p_*$ be any global minimizer. Then $q(p_*)=q(p)$,
where $p$ is the constructed minimizer, and $p_*$ is feasible. Applying the
identity in step 2.1 with $v=p_*$ expresses zero as the sum of two
nonnegative terms. In particular, for $H:=B+\lambda I$,
$(p_*-p)^TH(p_*-p)=0$. By [F2], diagonalize the symmetric positive
semidefinite matrix $H$ from step 2.1. In these coordinates the last
quadratic form is $\sum_i\nu_iw_i^2=0$ with every $\nu_i\ge0$, so
$\nu_iw_i=0$ for every $i$ and $H(p_*-p)=0$. Since $Hp=-g$, this gives
$Hp_*=-g$. If $\lambda>0$, the other nonnegative term in the identity
vanishes only when $\|p_*\|_2=\Delta$; if $\lambda=0$, complementarity is
automatic. Thus $p_*$ satisfies all three conditions.

The constructed case $\lambda_0>0$ has $g\perp E_\mu$ and adds exactly
the missing boundary component in $E_\mu$; when its length is positive,
opposite choices of $z$ are distinct and the same inequality in step 2.1
proves both globally minimizing. This verifies the stated hard-case clause.

derivations.claim:
By [F2], write $B=U\operatorname{diag}(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_n)U^T$ with $U$
orthogonal. Positive definiteness [F1] gives $\mu_i>0$ for every unit
eigenvector. Thus $C=U\operatorname{diag}(1/\mu_1,\ldots,1/\mu_n)U^T$
satisfies $CB=BC=I$ and is a linear inverse by [F3]. Hence
$p_N=-Cg$ solves $Bp_N=-g$. If $p$ is another solution, then
$B(p-p_N)=0$, and applying $C$ gives $p=p_N$.

If $g=0$, [F4] returns $p=0$, which is feasible. Suppose $g\ne0$.
The Cauchy step exists by its explicit formula and is feasible by [F5], and
step 1.1 gives the unique Newton step. If $\|p_N\|_2\le\Delta$, the
algorithm returns the feasible $p_N$. If $\|p_N\|_2>\Delta$ but
$\|p_C\|_2=\Delta$, it returns the feasible $p_C$.

In the remaining branch, $\|p_N\|_2>\Delta$ and $\|p_C\|_2<\Delta$.
Put $d=p_N-p_C$ and
$q(t)=\|p_C+td\|_2^2-\Delta^2$. Then $q$ is a real quadratic polynomial,
$q(0)<0$, and $q(1)>0$. By [F6] it is continuous, and [F7] gives a root
$t\in(0,1)$. Its coefficients are
$a=\|d\|_2^2>0$, $b=2\langle p_C,d\rangle$, and
$c=\|p_C\|_2^2-\Delta^2<0$. Thus its discriminant
$b^2-4ac>b^2$, and the two roots have product $c/a<0$. Exactly one root is
positive, and the quadratic formula identifies it as
$(-b+\sqrt{b^2-4ac})/(2a)$. The root in $(0,1)$ is therefore exactly the
algorithm's scalar $t$. The vector $p_D=p_C+td$ has norm $\Delta$; the
final comparison returns either $p_D$ or $p_C$, both feasible.

Step 1.1 proves unique Newton-step existence, and steps 1.2–2.1 cover
every dogleg branch and establish its feasibility and root formula. The
Definition calls the Newton solve once on every nonstationary input, calls
the scalar-root formula only in branch 3, and has no iteration branch.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of

Let $n\ge1$.  A linear map $A:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$
([[def-euclidean-linear-map]]) is **invertible** when there is a linear map
$B:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ such that

$$B(Au)=u\quad\hbox{and}\quad A(Bu)=u\qquad(u\in\mathbb R^n).$$

The map $B$ is unique: if $C$ has the same two properties, then
$C=C\circ(A\circ B)=(C\circ A)\circ B=B$.  It is denoted $A^{-1}$.

$g$, symmetric model matrix $B$, and
radius $\Delta>0$. If $g=0$, return $p_C=0$ with status `stationary`. If
$g\ne0$, set $c:=g^TBg$ and define
$$\tau:=\begin{cases}
\Delta/\|g\|_2,&c\le0,\\
\min\{\|g\|_2^2/c,\ \Delta/\|g\|_2\},&c>0.
\end{cases}$$
Return $p_C:=-\tau g$ with status `step`.

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,
   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$
   where $I_n$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]];
   at $n=0$ the unique empty matrix $I_0\in M_0(\mathbb{R})$ has
   $\lVert I_0\rVert_p=0$, the convention of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n\ge1$, let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable at
$x\in\mathbb R^n$, and put $g:=\nabla f(x)$ using the gradient convention of
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. Let $B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be a
symmetric matrix and let $\Delta>0$. A quadratic model at $x$ is

$$m(p):=f(x)+\langle g,p\rangle+\tfrac12 p^TBp,\qquad p\in\mathbb R^n,$$

with the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]
and matrix products as in [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. The
trust-region ball is $\mathcal B_\Delta:=\{p:\|p\|_2\le\Delta\}$. The
predicted reduction of a feasible step $p\in\mathcal B_\Delta$ is
$\operatorname{pred}(p):=m(0)-m(p)$. Its actual reduction is
$\operatorname{ared}(p):=f(x)-f(x+p)$. When $\operatorname{pred}(p)>0$, the
actual-to-predicted reduction ratio is

$$\rho(p):=\frac{\operatorname{ared}(p)}{\operatorname{pred}(p)}.$$

The quantity $\|B\|_2$ means the matrix norm induced by the Euclidean vector
norm, namely the $p=2$ case of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]]. It is not required

approximations are both admitted. The ratio is undefined when predicted

fallback or return a failure status in that case.

derivations.claim:
Put $a:=\|g\|_2>0$, $c:=g^TBg$, and
$\psi(t):=m(-tg)-m(0)=-ta^2+\tfrac12t^2c$ on
$0\le t\le\Delta/a$. If $c\le0$, then for $t_2>t_1\ge0$,
$\psi(t_2)-\psi(t_1)=-(t_2-t_1)a^2+\tfrac12c(t_2^2-t_1^2)<0$; hence its
minimum is at $t=\Delta/a$, which is the first branch in [F1]. The predicted
reduction is $P\ge a\Delta\ge\tfrac12a\min\{\Delta,a/M\}$. This case
also covers $M=0$, since then $c=0$.

Suppose $c>0$. Completing the square in $\psi$ shows its unconstrained
minimizer is $t=a^2/c$, so its minimizer on the segment is
$\tau=\min\{a^2/c,\Delta/a\}$, the second branch in [F1]. Put $s:=\tau a$;
then $s=\min\{a^3/c,\Delta\}$ and $s\le a^3/c$. Thus
$P=as-\tfrac12(c/a^2)s^2\ge\tfrac12as$. By [F2] and [F3],
$c=\langle g,Bg\rangle\le a\|Bg\|_2\le Ma^2$, whence
$a^3/c\ge a/M$ and $s\ge\min\{\Delta,a/M\}$. Therefore
$P\ge\tfrac12a\min\{\Delta,a/M\}$.

The cases $c\le0$ and $c>0$ exhaust all real $c$. Both establish that
the algorithm returns the segment minimizer and prove the stated decrease
bound.

Input a model of [[def-trust-region-quadratic-model-and-ratio]], a finite
inner cap $J\in\mathbb N_0$, and a
residual tolerance $\tau_{tol}\ge0$. If $g=0$, return $0$ with status
`stationary`. Otherwise initialize $z_0=0$, $r_0=g$, $d_0=-r_0$, and $j=0$.
For at most $J$ inner iterations:

1. If $\|r_j\|_2\le\tau_{tol}$, take $z_j$ as the candidate and stop.
2. If $d_j=0$, take $z_j$ as the candidate and stop; the final comparison
   below then returns $p_C$ whenever $z_j$ does not give at least its model
   decrease.
3. Put $c_j:=d_j^TBd_j$. If $c_j\le0$, set
   $$t_j:=\frac{-\langle z_j,d_j\rangle+
   \sqrt{\langle z_j,d_j\rangle^2+\|d_j\|_2^2(\Delta^2-\|z_j\|_2^2)}}
   {\|d_j\|_2^2},$$
   take $z_j+t_jd_j$ as the candidate, and stop. This is the nonpositive
   curvature boundary exit.
4. Otherwise put $\alpha_j:=\|r_j\|_2^2/c_j$ and
   $\widehat z:=z_j+\alpha_jd_j$.
   If $\|\widehat z\|_2\ge\Delta$, use the same positive-root formula in
   step 3, take $z_j+t_jd_j$ as the candidate, and stop at the trust boundary.
5. Set $r_{j+1}:=r_j+\alpha_jBd_j$ and $z_{j+1}:=\widehat z$. If
   $\|r_{j+1}\|_2\le\tau_{tol}$, take $z_{j+1}$ as the candidate and stop.
   Otherwise set
   $$\beta_{j+1}:=\frac{\|r_{j+1}\|_2^2}{\|r_j\|_2^2},\qquad
   d_{j+1}:=-r_{j+1}+\beta_{j+1}d_j,$$
   and increase $j$ by one.

If the cap is reached, take the current $z_j$ as the candidate. In
all nonstationary cases compute the Cauchy step $p_C$ and compare model values:
return the candidate if its model value is no greater than $m(p_C)$, and
otherwise return $p_C$. Thus a capped or unhelpful inner recurrence still
returns the selected candidate or Cauchy step.

$$K_m(A,b):=\operatorname{span}\{b,Ab,\dots,A^{m-1}b\}.$$

Thus $K_m(A,b)\subseteq K_{m+1}(A,b)$ for every $m\ge 0$.

derivations.claim:
Initially, $z_0=0\in K_0(B,-g)$, while $r_0=g\in K_1(B,-g)$ and
$d_0=-g\in K_1(B,-g)$. Also $\|z_0\|_2=0<\Delta$.

Suppose the algorithm makes an interior update at index $j$. By [F2],
$Bd_j\in K_{j+2}$, while $z_j\in K_j\subseteq K_{j+1}$ and
$r_j,d_j\in K_{j+1}$. The first two recurrences in [F1] therefore give
$z_{j+1}\in K_{j+1}$ and $r_{j+1}\in K_{j+2}$. The last recurrence gives
$d_{j+1}\in K_{j+2}$. The update is made only when
$\|\widehat z\|_2<\Delta$, so $z_{j+1}$ remains strictly inside the ball.

At a boundary exit, put $z=z_j$, $d=d_j$,
$a=\|d\|_2^2$, $b=\langle z,d\rangle$, and
$c=\|z\|_2^2-\Delta^2$. Steps 1.1–1.2 show $\|z\|_2<\Delta$, and the
zero-direction guard in [F1] gives $d\ne0$, so $a>0$ and $c<0$. The
boundary equation is
$$a t^2+2bt+c=0.$$
Its discriminant is $4(b^2-ac)>4b^2$, and the product of its roots is
$c/a<0$. Thus it has exactly one positive root, namely
$$t=\frac{-b+\sqrt{b^2+a(\Delta^2-\|z\|_2^2)}}{a},$$
which is the algorithm's formula. In the positive-curvature exit, the
unconstrained point $\widehat z=z+\alpha_jd$ satisfies
$\|\widehat z\|_2\ge\Delta$, so the quadratic is nonnegative at
$\alpha_j$. It is negative on $[0,t_+)$, where $t_+$ is its unique positive
root; hence $t_+\le\alpha_j$. In either boundary branch,
$\|z+t_+d\|_2=\Delta$.

Before a non-boundary stop, the current recurrence vector is strictly
inside the ball by steps 1.1–1.2. Thus residual-tolerance and zero-direction
stops, and the inner-cap stop, use a feasible current vector. A boundary stop
uses a vector of norm $\Delta$ by step 2.1. The stationary branch returns
zero, and the final comparison returns either its feasible candidate or the
Cauchy step, which is feasible because [F3] gives
$\|p_C\|_2=\tau\|g\|_2\le\Delta$. Hence every returned vector is feasible.

Induction on the interior updates proves the claimed Krylov memberships.
The base case is step 1.1, and the induction step is step 1.2.

Input an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a twice continuously
differentiable $f:U\to\mathbb R$, an initial point $x_0\in U$, target
$\varepsilon\ge0$, outer trial cap $N\in\mathbb N_0$, and an exact-Hessian
cubic-model solver $S$. Other inputs are $0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$,

vector. A proposed vector is admissible when it passes the model-solution
checks below. The solver may return `no-candidate` if it cannot certify such
a vector within its cap. Exact global minimizers are an admissible special
case; the local criterion also permits inexact steps satisfying the stated
conditions of [[lem-global-cubic-model-minimizer-decrease]].

The output is the last accepted iterate and one of `stationary`,
`target-achieved`, `outer-budget-exhausted`, `model-solver-failure`,
`inconsistent-model-solver`, `domain-exit`, or
`regularization-cap-exhausted`.

1. Compute $g_k:=\nabla f(x_k)$. If $g_k=0$, return $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$.
   If $\|g_k\|_2\le\varepsilon$, return $(x_k,\texttt{target-achieved})$.
   If $k=N$, return $(x_k,\texttt{outer-budget-exhausted})$.

   $m_k(s)=f(x_k)+\langle g_k,s\rangle+\tfrac12s^TB_ks+
   \tfrac{\sigma_k}{3}\|s\|_2^3$ of
   [[def-adaptive-cubic-regularization-model]]. By
   [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]], $B_k$ is symmetric. Put
   $a_k:=\|g_k\|_2$, $q_k:=g_k^TB_kg_k$, and compute the cubic Cauchy
   step
   $$s_{C,k}:=-t_{C,k}g_k,\qquad
   t_{C,k}:=\frac{-q_k+\sqrt{q_k^2+4\sigma_ka_k^5}}
   {2\sigma_ka_k^3}.$$

   $(x_k,\texttt{model-solver-failure})$. For a proposed $s_k$, recompute
   $\operatorname{pred}_k:=m_k(0)-m_k(s_k)$ and
   $\nabla m_k(s_k):=g_k+B_ks_k+\sigma_k\|s_k\|_2s_k$. Check

   \qquad s_k^TB_ks_k+\sigma_k\|s_k\|_2^3\ge0,$$

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For every real $x\ge1$, the natural logarithm of
[[def-natural-logarithm]] satisfies
$$0\le\log x\le x-1\le x.$$

for every $x \in F$ there is a natural number $n \ge 1$ with $x < n \cdot 1_F$,
where $n \cdot 1_F$ is the canonical natural of the ordered field $F$
([[def-ordered-field]]). Equivalently, the canonical naturals are cofinal in $F$.

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor

derivations.claim:
Let $\bar\delta_\varepsilon:=
\min\{c_\delta\varepsilon,\Delta_{max}\}$. Every radius during a
pre-target trial is at least
$$r_\varepsilon=\min\{\Delta_0,\gamma_{dec}\bar\delta_\varepsilon\}>0.$$
Indeed, this holds initially. If a trial is rejected, [F3] implies its
radius exceeded $\bar\delta_\varepsilon$, since at or below that threshold
the ratio is at least $\eta_2$; after multiplication by $\gamma_{dec}$ the
new radius is greater than $\gamma_{dec}\bar\delta_\varepsilon$. An
accepted update does not decrease the radius. Induction proves the bound.

If the target were never reached, every rejection block would be finite:
an infinite block would multiply a fixed radius by $\gamma_{dec}^j\to0$ by
[F8], eventually making $\Delta\le\bar\delta_\varepsilon$, where [F3]
forbids rejection. Thus an infinite pre-target run would contain infinitely
many accepted trials. For any accepted trial its starting gradient norm
$a$ exceeds $\varepsilon$. From step 1.1,
$\Delta_k\ge r_\varepsilon\ge c_R\varepsilon$, because
$\varepsilon\le1$ and
$$\min\{c_\delta\varepsilon,\Delta_{max}\}
\ge\varepsilon\min\{c_\delta,\Delta_{max}\}.$$
Since $\Delta_0\ge\varepsilon\Delta_0$, taking the minimum with
$\Delta_0$ in the definition of $r_\varepsilon$ gives
$r_\varepsilon\ge c_R\varepsilon$.
Also $a/\|B_k\|_2\ge\varepsilon/M_B$, with the stated infinity
convention if $M_B=0$. Hence
$$\min\{\Delta_k,a/\|B_k\|_2\}\ge c_P\varepsilon.$$
By [F1] and [F2], the predicted reduction is at least
$\tfrac12\theta_Cc_P\varepsilon^2$. Acceptance gives actual decrease at
least $\eta_1$ times this amount, namely $c_S\varepsilon^2$. If the target
were never reached, after $m$ accepted trials the objective would be at most
$f(x_0)-m c_S\varepsilon^2$. By [F7] choose an integer
$m>(f(x_0)-f_{inf})/(c_S\varepsilon^2)$; this contradicts [A3]. Therefore
the target is reached after finitely many accepted trials. Summing their
decreases gives
$N_s c_S\varepsilon^2\le f(x_0)-f_{inf}$, the claimed successful-step
bound.

Let $\Delta_T$ be the radius after the accepted trial that first
reaches the target. Each rejected trial multiplies the radius by
$\gamma_{dec}$; each accepted update multiplies it by some
$r_j\in[1,\gamma_{inc}]$. Therefore
$$\Delta_T=\Delta_0\gamma_{dec}^{N_u}\prod_{j=1}^{N_s}r_j.$$
Step 1.1 gives $\Delta_T\ge r_\varepsilon$. By [F5],
$\log\gamma_{dec}<0$, and logarithms of positive products give
$$\log\Delta_T=\log\Delta_0+N_u\log\gamma_{dec}
+\sum_{j=1}^{N_s}\log r_j.$$
Rearranging and using $\log r_j\le\log\gamma_{inc}$ yields
$$N_u|\log\gamma_{dec}|
=\log(\Delta_0/\Delta_T)+\sum_{j=1}^{N_s}\log r_j
\le\log(\Delta_0/r_\varepsilon)+N_s\log\gamma_{inc},$$
which proves the rejection bound, including every rejected trial.

Since $r_\varepsilon\ge c_R\varepsilon$ for
$0<\varepsilon\le1$, [F5] gives
$$\log(\Delta_0/r_\varepsilon)
\le\log(\Delta_0/(c_R\varepsilon))
=\log(\Delta_0/c_R)+\log(1/\varepsilon).$$
By [F6], $\log(1/\varepsilon)\le1/\varepsilon$; since
$0<\varepsilon\le1$, $1/\varepsilon\le1/\varepsilon^2$. Thus the radius
term is $O(\varepsilon^{-2})$, as is $N_s$ by step 1.2, so
$N_s+N_u=O(\varepsilon^{-2})$. If the finite outer cap
allows at least that many trials, the process reaches the target before the
cap.

For any nonstationary trial, $\|g_k\|_2>0$ and $\Delta_k>0$.
By [F2], the Cauchy step has $P_C>0$. The selection rule either chooses a
candidate with predicted decrease at least $\theta_C P_C$, or uses $p_C$;
the small-radius override also uses $p_C$. Since $0<\theta_C\le1$, every
branch therefore gives $P_k\ge\theta_C P_C>0$, so the ratio in the
algorithm is defined.

On an accepted trial, $\rho_k\ge\eta_1>0$ and $P_k>0$ by step 3.1.
Thus $f(x_{k+1})=f(x_k)-\rho_kP_k<f(x_k)$, proving strict decrease at every
accepted trial.

an initial radius $0<\Delta_0\le\Delta_{max}$, a trial cap
$N\in\mathbb N_0$, a target $\varepsilon\ge0$, constants
$0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$, $0<\gamma_{dec}<1<\gamma_{inc}$,
$0<\theta_C\le1$, and a declared model-Hessian bound $M_B\ge0$. At each
trial $k$, the supplied symmetric model matrix $B_k$ must satisfy
$\|B_k\|_2\le M_B$. A finite-budget subproblem routine $S$ returns either a
vector or `failure`; its output is treated only as a candidate and is not
assumed to minimize the trust-region model. The output is the last accepted
point and one of `stationary`, `target-achieved`, `outer-budget-exhausted`,
or `model-evaluation-failure`.

For $k=0,1,\ldots,N$, in order:

1. Set $g_k:=\nabla f(x_k)$. If $g_k=0$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$. If $\|g_k\|_2\le\varepsilon$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{target-achieved})$. If $k=N$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{outer-budget-exhausted})$.
2. Form $m_k$ from [[def-trust-region-quadratic-model-and-ratio]], compute
   the Cauchy step $p_C$ from [[alg-trust-region-cauchy-step]], and set
   $P_C:=m_k(0)-m_k(p_C)>0$. Query $S$ with this model and radius. Use its
   candidate $q$ only if it is feasible and
   $m_k(0)-m_k(q)\ge\theta_C P_C$; otherwise set $p:=p_C$. If it qualifies,
   set $p:=q$. If $M_B=0$, interpret $\|g_k\|_2/(2M_B)=+\infty$. Whenever
   $\Delta_k\le\|g_k\|_2/(2M_B)$, replace the candidate by $p:=p_C$.

   return $(x_k,\texttt{model-evaluation-failure})$.

\min\{\Delta,\|g\|_2/M\}.$$

citations.quote:
Input an open set $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, a twice continuously
differentiable $f:U\to\mathbb R$, an initial point $x_0\in U$, target
$\varepsilon\ge0$, outer trial cap $N\in\mathbb N_0$, and an exact-Hessian
cubic-model solver $S$. Other inputs are $0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$,
$\gamma_{up}>1$, $0<\gamma_{down}<1$, $0<\kappa<1$,
$0<\sigma_{min}\le\sigma_0\le\sigma_{max}$, $0<\kappa_\theta<1$,
and the finite inner cap $J\in\mathbb N_0$. On input of the model, $J$,
and $\kappa_\theta$, the solver $S$ returns `no-candidate` or proposes a
vector. A proposed vector is admissible when it passes the model-solution
checks below. The solver may return `no-candidate` if it cannot certify such
a vector within its cap. Exact global minimizers are an admissible special
case; the local criterion also permits inexact steps satisfying the stated
conditions of [[lem-global-cubic-model-minimizer-decrease]].

The output is the last accepted iterate and one of `stationary`,
`target-achieved`, `outer-budget-exhausted`, `model-solver-failure`,
`inconsistent-model-solver`, `domain-exit`, or
`regularization-cap-exhausted`.

For $k=0,1,\ldots,N$, in order:

1. Compute $g_k:=\nabla f(x_k)$. If $g_k=0$, return $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$.
   If $\|g_k\|_2\le\varepsilon$, return $(x_k,\texttt{target-achieved})$.
   If $k=N$, return $(x_k,\texttt{outer-budget-exhausted})$.
2. Set $B_k:=\nabla^2 f(x_k)$ and form the model
   $m_k(s)=f(x_k)+\langle g_k,s\rangle+\tfrac12s^TB_ks+
   \tfrac{\sigma_k}{3}\|s\|_2^3$ of
   [[def-adaptive-cubic-regularization-model]]. By
   [[cor-hessian-is-symmetric]], $B_k$ is symmetric. Put
   $a_k:=\|g_k\|_2$, $q_k:=g_k^TB_kg_k$, and compute the cubic Cauchy
   step
   $$s_{C,k}:=-t_{C,k}g_k,\qquad
   t_{C,k}:=\frac{-q_k+\sqrt{q_k^2+4\sigma_ka_k^5}}
   {2\sigma_ka_k^3}.$$
   Call $S(m_k,J,\kappa_\theta)$. If it returns `no-candidate`, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{model-solver-failure})$. For a proposed $s_k$, recompute
   $\operatorname{pred}_k:=m_k(0)-m_k(s_k)$ and
   $\nabla m_k(s_k):=g_k+B_ks_k+\sigma_k\|s_k\|_2s_k$. Check
   $$g_k^Ts_k+s_k^TB_ks_k+\sigma_k\|s_k\|_2^3=0,
   \qquad s_k^TB_ks_k+\sigma_k\|s_k\|_2^3\ge0,$$
   $$\|\nabla m_k(s_k)\|_2\le
   \kappa_\theta\min\{1,\|s_k\|_2\}\|g_k\|_2,
   \qquad m_k(s_k)\le m_k(s_{C,k}).$$
   If any check fails, or if $s_k=0$ or
   $\operatorname{pred}_k\le0$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{inconsistent-model-solver})$.
3. If $x_k+s_k\notin U$, return $(x_k,\texttt{domain-exit})$ without
   evaluating $f$ there. Otherwise evaluate $f(x_k+s_k)$ and set
   $\rho_k:=[f(x_k)-f(x_k+s_k)]/\operatorname{pred}_k$.
   If $\rho_k<\eta_1$, reject the step and keep $x_{k+1}:=x_k$. If
   $\sigma_k=\sigma_{max}$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{regularization-cap-exhausted})$; otherwise set
   $\sigma_{k+1}:=\min\{\gamma_{up}\sigma_k,\sigma_{max}\}$ and continue.
4. If $\rho_k\ge\eta_1$, accept and set $x_{k+1}:=x_k+s_k$. If
   $\rho_k>\eta_2$ and
   $\|s_k\|_2\ge\kappa\|g_k\|_2/\sigma_k$, set
   $\sigma_{k+1}:=\max\{\sigma_{min},\gamma_{down}\sigma_k\}$;
   otherwise set $\sigma_{k+1}:=\sigma_k$.

The finite cap, solver failure, inconsistent-solver, domain-exit, and
regularization-cap branches are explicit. The model-solution checks include
the two cubic conditions (4.1)–(4.2), residual condition TC.s, and the
Cauchy-model decrease condition of Cartis–Gould–Toint, Part II, §4. The
procedure alone makes no unconditional convergence or evaluation-complexity
claim.

For the cubic model $m_\sigma$ of [[def-adaptive-cubic-regularization-model]],
with $\sigma>0$ and symmetric $B$, a global minimizer exists. If $g\ne0$ and
$s_*$ is any global minimizer, then $s_*\ne0$ and
$$g+Bs_*+\sigma\|s_*\|_2s_*=0,$$
$$m_\sigma(0)-m_\sigma(s_*)\ge\frac{\sigma}{6}\|s_*\|_2^3.$$

More generally, every $s$ satisfying
$$g^Ts+s^TBs+\sigma\|s\|_2^3=0,\qquad
s^TBs+\sigma\|s\|_2^3\ge0$$
has $m_\sigma(0)-m_\sigma(s)\ge\frac{\sigma}{6}\|s\|_2^3$.
For $g\ne0$, put $a=\|g\|_2$ and $q=g^TBg$. The unique minimizer of
the cubic model on the negative-gradient ray $\{-tg:t\ge0\}$ is
$$s_C=-t_Cg,\qquad
t_C=\frac{-q+\sqrt{q^2+4\sigma a^5}}{2\sigma a^3}>0.$$

Suppose $f$ is $C^2$ and its Hessian is $L$-Lipschitz on each trial segment,
meaning
$$\|\nabla^2f(u)-\nabla^2f(v)\|_2\le L\|u-v\|_2.$$
Run [[alg-adaptive-cubic-regularization]] with exact Hessians, and assume each
trial on which a ratio is evaluated uses either an exact global cubic-model
minimizer or a candidate passing the algorithm's cubic solution, residual, and
Cauchy-decrease checks, together with
$0<\sigma_{min}\le\sigma_k\le\sigma_{max}$ and $\sigma_{max}\ge3L$.
Then no ratio-based rejection occurs when $\sigma_k\ge3L$. If
$\gamma_{up}>1$, let $R\in\mathbb N_0$ satisfy
$\gamma_{up}^R\sigma_{min}\ge3L$; such an $R$ exists. Every block of
consecutive ratio-based rejected trials has length at most $R$.
For a $C^2$ scalar field $f$, $H_f(a)^T=H_f(a)$ at every point $a$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,
   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$
   where $I_n$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]];
   at $n=0$ the unique empty matrix $I_0\in M_0(\mathbb{R})$ has
   $\lVert I_0\rVert_p=0$, the convention of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so

6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular

inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

On any trial segment, put $s=s_k$ and, for each coordinate $i$, let
$e_i$ be its standard basis vector and
$$r_i(t):=e_i^T\big(\nabla f(x_k+ts)-g_k-tB_ks\big),
\qquad 0\le t\le1.$$
Since $B_k=\nabla^2f(x_k)$ by the algorithm and [F4] confirms its symmetry,
$r_i(0)=0$ and
$$r_i'(t)=e_i^T\big(\nabla^2f(x_k+ts)-B_k\big)s.$$
By [A1], [F6], [F7], and [F8], $|r_i'(t)|\le Lt\|s\|_2^2$. Applying [F5] to
$r_i$ on $[0,1]$ gives $|r_i(1)|\le L\|s\|_2^2$. Consequently,
$$\|\nabla f(x_k+s)-g_k-B_ks\|_2\le\sqrt n L\|s\|_2^2.$$

condition in [F2] and step 1.1 yield
$$\|\nabla f(x_{k+1})\|_2
\le(\sigma_k+\sqrt n L)\|s_k\|_2^2

accepted trials and using [A2] bounds their number by

is no rejected block after the first stationary or target-achieved iterate,
so $N_u\le R N_s$. In case 1 this gives
$$N_s+N_u\le(R+1)\left(\frac{f(x_0)-f_{inf}}
{c_g\varepsilon^{3/2}}+1\right).$$

$$\|g+B_ks+\sigma_k r s\|_2
\le\kappa_\theta\min\{1,r\}\|g\|_2.$$

$$\|g^+\|_2\le(\sigma_{max}+\sqrt n L)r^2

By the $K$-Lipschitz gradient assumption,

$$ (1-\kappa_\theta\min\{1,r\})\|g^+\|_2
\le(\sigma_{max}+\sqrt n L+\kappa_\theta K)r^2.$$

decrease conclusion of [F2] gives predicted reduction greater than

differentiable $f:U\to\mathbb R$, an initial point $x_0\in U$, target
$\varepsilon\ge0$, outer trial cap $N\in\mathbb N_0$, and an exact-Hessian
cubic-model solver $S$. On an input model and finite inner cap $J\in\mathbb N$,
$S$ returns either `no-candidate` or a global minimizer of that model; the
solver is permitted to return `no-candidate` if it cannot certify a minimizer
within its cap. Other inputs are $0<\eta_1<\eta_2<1$,
$\gamma_{up}>1$, $0<\gamma_{down}<1$, $0<\kappa<1$,
$0<\sigma_{min}\le\sigma_0\le\sigma_{max}$, and the inner cap $J$.
The output is the last accepted iterate and one of `stationary`,
`target-achieved`, `outer-budget-exhausted`, `model-solver-failure`,
`inconsistent-model-solver`, or `regularization-cap-exhausted`.

For $k=0,1,\ldots,N$, in order:

1. Compute $g_k:=\nabla f(x_k)$. If $g_k=0$, return $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$.
   If $\|g_k\|_2\le\varepsilon$, return $(x_k,\texttt{target-achieved})$.
   If $k=N$, return $(x_k,\texttt{outer-budget-exhausted})$.
2. Set $B_k:=\nabla^2 f(x_k)$ and form the model
   $m_k(s)=f(x_k)+\langle g_k,s\rangle+\tfrac12s^TB_ks+
   \tfrac{\sigma_k}{3}\|s\|_2^3$ of
   [[def-adaptive-cubic-regularization-model]]. Call $S(m_k,J)$. If it returns
   `no-candidate`, return $(x_k,\texttt{model-solver-failure})$. For a
   returned $s_k$, recompute $\operatorname{pred}_k:=m_k(0)-m_k(s_k)$. If
   $s_k=0$ or $\operatorname{pred}_k\le0$ while $g_k\ne0$, return
   `inconsistent-model-solver`.
3. Evaluate $f(x_k+s_k)$ and set
   $\rho_k:=[f(x_k)-f(x_k+s_k)]/\operatorname{pred}_k$.
   If $\rho_k<\eta_1$, reject the step and keep $x_{k+1}:=x_k$. If
   $\sigma_k=\sigma_{max}$, return
   $(x_k,\texttt{regularization-cap-exhausted})$; otherwise set
   $\sigma_{k+1}:=\min\{\gamma_{up}\sigma_k,\sigma_{max}\}$ and continue.
4. If $\rho_k\ge\eta_1$, accept and set $x_{k+1}:=x_k+s_k$. If
   $\rho_k>\eta_2$ and
   $\|s_k\|_2\ge\kappa\|g_k\|_2/\sigma_k$, set
   $\sigma_{k+1}:=\max\{\sigma_{min},\gamma_{down}\sigma_k\}$;
   otherwise set $\sigma_{k+1}:=\sigma_k$.

budget always succeeds. The global-minimizer decrease estimate is supplied by
[[lem-global-cubic-model-minimizer-decrease]]. This procedure alone makes no
unconditional convergence or evaluation-complexity claim.

For the cubic model $m_\sigma$ of [[def-adaptive-cubic-regularization-model]],
with $\sigma>0$ and symmetric $B$, a global minimizer exists. If $g\ne0$ and
$s_*$ is any global minimizer, then $s_*\ne0$ and
$$g+Bs_*+\sigma\|s_*\|_2s_*=0,$$

Suppose $f$ is $C^2$ and its Hessian is $L$-Lipschitz on each trial segment,
meaning
$$\|\nabla^2f(u)-\nabla^2f(v)\|_2\le L\|u-v\|_2.$$
Run [[alg-adaptive-cubic-regularization]] with exact Hessians, an exact global
minimizer of each cubic model on every solver-success trial,
$0<\sigma_{min}\le\sigma_k\le\sigma_{max}$, and $\sigma_{max}\ge3L$.

$\gamma_{up}>1$, let $R\in\mathbb N_0$ satisfy
$\gamma_{up}^R\sigma_{min}\ge3L$; such an $R$ exists. Every block of
consecutive ratio-based rejected trials has length at most $R$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

Let $n\ge1$, let $f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable at
$x\in\mathbb R^n$, and put $g:=\nabla f(x)$ using the gradient convention of
[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]. Let $B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be a
symmetric matrix and let $\Delta>0$. A quadratic model at $x$ is

$$m(p):=f(x)+\langle g,p\rangle+\tfrac12 p^TBp,\qquad p\in\mathbb R^n,$$

with the Euclidean inner product and norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]
and matrix products as in [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. The
trust-region ball is $\mathcal B_\Delta:=\{p:\|p\|_2\le\Delta\}$. The
predicted reduction of a feasible step $p\in\mathcal B_\Delta$ is
$\operatorname{pred}(p):=m(0)-m(p)$. Its actual reduction is
$\operatorname{ared}(p):=f(x)-f(x+p)$. When $\operatorname{pred}(p)>0$, the
actual-to-predicted reduction ratio is

$$\rho(p):=\frac{\operatorname{ared}(p)}{\operatorname{pred}(p)}.$$

The quantity $\|B\|_2$ means the matrix norm induced by the Euclidean vector
norm, namely the $p=2$ case of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]]. It is not required
that $B=\nabla^2f(x)$ in this definition; exact Hessians and symmetric model
approximations are both admitted. The ratio is undefined when predicted
reduction is nonpositive, so an algorithm must use a separately justified
fallback or return a failure status in that case.

Let $B\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ be symmetric, let $g\in\mathbb R^n$, and
let $\Delta>0$. Every global minimizer $p_*$ of
$$q(p):=\langle g,p\rangle+\tfrac12p^TBp\quad\text{over }\|p\|_2\le\Delta$$
has a multiplier $\lambda\ge0$ such that
$$ (B+\lambda I)p_*=-g,\qquad B+\lambda I\succeq0,\qquad
\lambda(\Delta-\|p_*\|_2)=0. $$
Conversely, every feasible $p_*$ satisfying these conditions is a global
minimizer. A global minimizer always exists.

The singular hard case is included as follows. Let $\mu$ be the least
eigenvalue of $B$ and $E_\mu$ its eigenspace. If $\mu<0$, $g\perp E_\mu$,
and the solution $p_0$ of
$(B-\mu I)p_0=-g$, $p_0\perp E_\mu$, has $\|p_0\|_2\le\Delta$, then
$$p_*=p_0+z,\qquad z\in E_\mu,\qquad
\|z\|_2^2=\Delta^2-\|p_0\|_2^2$$
is a global minimizer with the singular multiplier $\lambda=-\mu$. If
$\|p_0\|_2<\Delta$, both signs of any chosen nonzero $z$ of the required
length give distinct minimizers.

Input a model of [[def-trust-region-quadratic-model-and-ratio]] with gradient
$g$, symmetric model matrix $B$, and
radius $\Delta>0$. If $g=0$, return $p_C=0$ with status `stationary`. If
$g\ne0$, set $c:=g^TBg$ and define
$$\tau:=\begin{cases}
\Delta/\|g\|_2,&c\le0,\\
\min\{\|g\|_2^2/c,\ \Delta/\|g\|_2\},&c>0.
\end{cases}$$
Return $p_C:=-\tau g$ with status `step`.

$\sqrt5-2/5<2$; the strict inequality follows from $\sqrt5<12/5$.

be twice continuously differentiable, meaning that $f$ is $C^1$ and its
gradient is $C^1$.

[[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and
[[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. The identity matrix $I_n$ and
matrix-vector products have the convention of

model of [[def-matrix-free-access-model-for-krylov-methods]] for products

**Linear-solver input:** a fixed deterministic Krylov procedure $K$ which accepts a
matrix-free linear operator $A$, a right-hand side $b$, a tolerance $\tau\ge0$,
and a finite inner-iteration budget $M\in\mathbb N_0$. It returns either
`no-candidate` or `candidate` with a vector $p$ and an iteration count
$m\in\{0,1,\ldots,M\}$ satisfying $p\in K_m(A,b)$, where $K_m$ is as defined
by [[def-krylov-subspace-of-a-matrix-and-start-vector]]. A candidate's residual
status is never trusted: this algorithm recomputes
the requested residual using the supplied operator. **Other inputs:** $x_0\in U$, outer update budget
$N\in\mathbb N_0$, forcing values $\eta_k\in[0,\bar\eta]$ for a fixed
$0\le\bar\eta<1$, descent parameter $\sigma\in(0,1)$, regularization factor
$\gamma>1$, initial shift $\lambda_0>0$, shift cap $\lambda_{\max}\ge\lambda_0$,
regularized-attempt budget $J\in\mathbb N_0$, inner budget $M$, and the
parameters and finite expansion/zoom budgets of
[[alg-bracketing-zoom-strong-wolfe-search]]. **Output:** the last valid
iterate and one of `stationary`, `iteration-budget-exhausted`,
`no-descent-direction`, or `line-search-failure`; in the last case also
return the underlying line-search failure cause.

At iteration $k=0,1,\ldots,N$:

1. Compute $g_k:=g(x_k)$. If $g_k=0$, return $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$.
   If $k=N$, return $(x_k,\texttt{iteration-budget-exhausted})$.
2. Set $\lambda:=0$. For $j=0,1,\ldots,J$, call $K$ on
   $A_\lambda v:=H(x_k)v+\lambda I_nv$, right-hand side $-g_k$, tolerance
   $\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$, and budget $M$. A `no-candidate` result is a rejected
   attempt. If it returns a candidate $p$, compute
   $r:=(H(x_k)+\lambda I_n)p+g_k$. Accept this linear solve only when
   $\|r\|_2\le\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$ and
   $\langle g_k,p\rangle<-\sigma\|g_k\|_2\|p\|_2$; otherwise reject it.
   If the attempt is rejected and either $j=J$ or $\lambda=\lambda_{\max}$, stop the
   regularization loop. Otherwise set
   $\lambda:=\min\{\lambda_{\max},\lambda_0\}$ when $\lambda=0$, and
   $\lambda:=\min\{\lambda_{\max},\gamma\lambda\}$ when $\lambda>0$;
   then continue with the next $j$.
3. If no regularized attempt was accepted, set $p:=-g_k$ and check
   $\langle g_k,p\rangle<-\sigma\|g_k\|_2\|p\|_2$. If this check fails,
   return `no-descent-direction`. For the stated $\sigma$ and $g_k\ne0$ it
   passes, but the check remains part of the procedure.

   If it returns failure, return $(x_k,\texttt{line-search-failure},s)$, where $s$ is
   the returned line-search failure cause. Otherwise, for its returned strong Wolfe step $t_k$,
   set $x_{k+1}:=x_k+t_kp$ and continue.

$\|H(x_k)p+g_k\|_2\le\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$. A regularized attempt checks the
residual for the shifted system instead. Finite inner, regularization, and
line-search budgets can return failure; the procedure makes no global
convergence claim. The local rate theorem applies only to an unshifted
$\lambda=0$ sequence taking full steps $t_k=1$ and remaining in its stated
local tube. This algorithm does not assert that every run enters that branch.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:D\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$
([[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]), let $x\in D$, and let
$p\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$. Define the open parameter set $S_{x,p}:=\{t\in\mathbb R:x+tp\in D\}$,
which contains $0$, the feasible ray $T_{x,p}:=S_{x,p}\cap[0,\infty)$,
and $\phi(t):=f(x+tp)$ for $t\in S_{x,p}$. At every $t\in S_{x,p}$,
including $0$, the chain rule gives $\phi'(t)=Df(x+tp)p$.
By [[thm-total-derivative-computes-directional-and-partial-derivatives]],
the matrix of $Df$ is the Jacobian, whose scalar-field row is the transpose
of the gradient. Hence
$\phi'(t)=\langle\nabla f(x+tp),p\rangle$, using the gradient convention
of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the Euclidean inner product of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A direction is a **descent direction** at
$x$ when $\phi'(0)=\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle<0$.

Assume for the line-search conditions below that $p$ is a descent direction
at $x$.
Fix constants $0<c_1<c_2<1/2$. A feasible step $t>0$ is a **Wolfe step**
when
$$
\phi(t)\le\phi(0)+c_1t\phi'(0),\qquad \phi'(t)\ge c_2\phi'(0).
$$
It is a **strong Wolfe step** when it satisfies the first inequality and
$$
|\phi'(t)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|.
$$
The first inequality is the Armijo sufficient-decrease condition. The second
Wolfe inequality is the curvature condition. Every strong Wolfe step is a
Wolfe step, because $\phi'(0)<0$ and the strong curvature bound implies
$\phi'(t)\ge-c_2|\phi'(0)|=c_2\phi'(0)$.

For a descent direction define its **descent angle** $\theta\in[0,\pi/2)$ by
$$
\cos\theta:=-\frac{\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle}{\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\|p\|_2}.
$$
The denominator is nonzero for a descent direction. The Cauchy–Schwarz
inequality [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]] ensures $0<\cos\theta\le1$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:D\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$,
let $x\in D$, and let $p\in\mathbb R^n$ be arbitrary. Fix $0<c_1<c_2<1/2$ and finite
budgets $E,Z\in\mathbb N$ for expansion and zoom trials. After the direction check passes, use the functions
$\phi(t)=f(x+tp)$ and $\phi'(t)=\langle\nabla f(x+tp),p\rangle$ from
[[def-wolfe-and-strong-wolfe-conditions]]. **Output:** either a positive
strong Wolfe step, or one of `invalid-direction`, `domain-exit`, and
`evaluation-budget-exhausted`.

1. If $\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle\ge0$, return `invalid-direction`.
   Set $a:=0$ and $t:=1$. For at most $E$ expansion trials, in order:
   - If $x+tp\notin D$, return `domain-exit` without evaluating the trial.
   - Evaluate $\phi(t)$ and $\phi'(t)$. If
     $\phi(t)>\phi(0)+c_1t\phi'(0)$ or $\phi(t)\ge\phi(a)$, call the zoom
     procedure below with the ordered endpoint pair $(a,t)$ and return its
     output.
   - If $|\phi'(t)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|$, return $t$ as a strong Wolfe step.
   - If $\phi'(t)\ge0$, call zoom with the reversed endpoint pair $(t,a)$ and
     return its output.
   - Otherwise set $a:=t$ and $t:=2t$.
2. If the expansion budget is exhausted, return `evaluation-budget-exhausted`.

For `zoom(a,b)`, preserve the endpoint order even when $b<a$. For at most
$Z$ zoom trials, in order:

1. Set $m:=(a+b)/2$. If $x+mp\notin D$, return `domain-exit` without
   evaluating the trial.
2. Evaluate $\phi(m)$ and $\phi'(m)$. If
   $\phi(m)>\phi(0)+c_1m\phi'(0)$ or $\phi(m)\ge\phi(a)$, set $b:=m$.
   Otherwise, if $|\phi'(m)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|$, return $m$ as a strong Wolfe
   step. In the remaining branch, if $\phi'(m)(b-a)\ge0$, first set
   $b:=a$; then set $a:=m$.
3. If the zoom budget is exhausted, return `evaluation-budget-exhausted`.

The procedure returns a step only after both strong Wolfe inequalities have
been checked. Finite budgets and domain exits may return failure even when a
strong Wolfe step exists; no convergence claim follows from the procedure
alone.

Let $A$ be a square matrix over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and let $b$ be a
vector of matching size. Define

$$K_0(A,b):=\{0\},$$

and for $m\ge 1$ define the $m$th **Krylov subspace**

$$K_m(A,b):=\operatorname{span}\{b,Ab,\dots,A^{m-1}b\}.$$

Thus $K_m(A,b)\subseteq K_{m+1}(A,b)$ for every $m\ge 0$.

derivations.claim: The matrix $B$ is invertible and the raw Newton solution is $p_N=-B^{-1}g=(-1,3)/\sqrt2$. Direct calculation gives $Bp_N+g=0$, $\|p_N\|_2=\sqrt5$, $g^Tp_N=-4$, $\|g\|_2\|p_N\|_2=5$, and the unrestricted model decrease at $p_N$ is $-g^Tp_N-\tfrac12p_N^TBp_N=2$. Also $-g=(1,3)/\sqrt2$ and $B(-g)=(-1,3)/\sqrt2$ are linearly independent, so [F8] gives $K_2(B,-g)=\mathbb R^2$. Put $V=[-g\ B(-g)]$; its determinant is $3$, so the projected matrix $V^TBV$ is invertible because its determinant is $\det(V)^2\det(B)=-9$. Solving $V^TBV y=V^T(-g)$ gives $p=Vy\in K_2$ with $B p+g$ orthogonal to $K_2=\mathbb R^2$, hence $Bp+g=0$ and $p=p_N$. Thus a deterministic two-dimensional Galerkin Krylov solver may return $p_N$. With $\eta_0=0$ and descent parameter $\sigma=1/2$, [F5]'s residual and strict descent tests pass because $0\le0$ and $-4<-5/2$.

We have $\|g\|_2^2=5$ and $g^TBg=4$. By [F3], $p_C=(1,3)/\sqrt{10}$ and $\|p_C\|_2=1$. Its predicted reduction is $$-g^Tp_C-\tfrac12p_C^TBp_C=\sqrt5-\tfrac25.$$ For truncated CG with residual tolerance zero and inner cap at least one, $d_0=-g$, $d_0^TBd_0=4$, and $\alpha_0=5/4$. The unconstrained point $\widehat z=-(5/4)g$ has norm $5\sqrt5/4>1$, so the boundary exit is $z_0+t_0d_0$ with $t_0=1/\sqrt5$. It equals $p_C$, and the final comparison in [F4] returns a step with the same predicted reduction $\sqrt5-2/5$.

For $\phi(t):=f(tp_N)$, direct substitution gives $\phi(t)=-4t+2t^2$ and $\phi'(t)=-4+4t$. Set $c_1=1/10$ and $c_2=1/4$. At $t=1$, $\phi(1)=-2\le-2/5=c_1\phi'(0)$ and $|\phi'(1)|=0\le1=c_2|\phi'(0)|$. Thus the full step satisfies [F6]; with expansion budget at least one, [F7] returns $t=1$.

The point $p_*=(1,1)/\sqrt2$ has norm one and $(B+2I)p_*=(1,3)/\sqrt2=-g$, while $B+2I=\operatorname{diag}(1,3)\succeq0$. By [F2], it is a global trust- region minimizer. Its predicted reduction is $-g^Tp_*-\tfrac12p_*^TBp_*=2$. The Cauchy decrease is strictly smaller because $\sqrt5<12/5$, which follows from $5<144/25$. Thus the raw Newton line-search step is accepted at full length, whereas the feasible Cauchy and truncated-CG steps have the strictly smaller reduction $\sqrt5-2/5<2$.

[[def-hessian-and-euclidean-critical-point]]. The identity matrix $I_n$ and
matrix-vector products have the convention of
[[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. Use the matrix-free access
model of [[def-matrix-free-access-model-for-krylov-methods]] for products
$v\mapsto(H(x)+\lambda I_nv)$.

**Linear-solver input:** a fixed deterministic Krylov procedure $K$ which accepts a
matrix-free linear operator $A$, a right-hand side $b$, a tolerance $\tau\ge0$,
and a finite inner-iteration budget $M\in\mathbb N_0$. It returns either
`no-candidate` or `candidate` with a vector $p$ and an iteration count
$m\in\{0,1,\ldots,M\}$ satisfying $p\in K_m(A,b)$, where $K_m$ is as defined
by [[def-krylov-subspace-of-a-matrix-and-start-vector]]. A candidate's residual
status is never trusted: this algorithm recomputes
the requested residual using the supplied operator. **Other inputs:** $x_0\in U$, outer update budget
$N\in\mathbb N_0$, forcing values $\eta_k\in[0,\bar\eta]$ for a fixed
$\bar\eta<1$, descent parameter $\sigma\in(0,1)$, regularization factor
$\gamma>1$, initial shift $\lambda_0>0$, shift cap $\lambda_{\max}\ge\lambda_0$,
regularized-attempt budget $J\in\mathbb N_0$, inner budget $M$, and the
parameters and finite expansion/zoom budgets of
[[alg-bracketing-zoom-strong-wolfe-search]]. **Output:** the last valid
iterate and one of `stationary`, `iteration-budget-exhausted`,
`no-descent-direction`, or `line-search-failure`.

At iteration $k=0,1,\ldots,N$:

1. Compute $g_k:=g(x_k)$. If $g_k=0$, return $(x_k,\texttt{stationary})$.
   If $k=N$, return $(x_k,\texttt{iteration-budget-exhausted})$.
2. Set $\lambda:=0$. For $j=0,1,\ldots,J$, call $K$ on
   $A_\lambda v:=H(x_k)v+\lambda I_nv$, right-hand side $-g_k$, tolerance
   $\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$, and budget $M$. A `no-candidate` result is a rejected
   attempt. If it returns a candidate $p$, compute
   $r:=(H(x_k)+\lambda I_n)p+g_k$. Accept this linear solve only when
   $\|r\|_2\le\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$ and
   $\langle g_k,p\rangle<-\sigma\|g_k\|_2\|p\|_2$; otherwise reject it.
   If the attempt is rejected and either $j=J$ or $\lambda=\lambda_{\max}$, stop the
   regularization loop. Otherwise set
   $\lambda:=\min\{\lambda_{\max},\lambda_0\}$ when $\lambda=0$, and
   $\lambda:=\min\{\lambda_{\max},\gamma\lambda\}$ when $\lambda>0$;
   then continue with the next $j$.
3. If no regularized attempt was accepted, set $p:=-g_k$ and check
   $\langle g_k,p\rangle<-\sigma\|g_k\|_2\|p\|_2$. If this check fails,
   return `no-descent-direction`. For the stated $\sigma$ and $g_k\ne0$ it
   passes, but the check remains part of the procedure.
4. Call [[alg-bracketing-zoom-strong-wolfe-search]] at $x_k$ in direction $p$.
   If it returns failure, return $(x_k,\texttt{line-search-failure})$ with
   that failure status. Otherwise, for its returned strong Wolfe step $t_k$,
   set $x_{k+1}:=x_k+t_kp$ and continue.

The first unregularized system uses the forcing residual
$\|H(x_k)p+g_k\|_2\le\eta_k\|g_k\|_2$. A regularized attempt checks the
residual for the shifted system instead. Finite inner, regularization, and
line-search budgets can return failure; the procedure makes no global
convergence claim. The local rate theorem applies only to an unshifted
$\lambda=0$ sequence taking full steps $t_k=1$ and remaining in its stated
local tube. This algorithm does not assert that every run enters that branch.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:D\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$
([[def-c-one-map-and-local-inverse]]), let $x\in D$, and let
$p\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$. Define the feasible ray
$T_{x,p}:=\{t\ge0:x+tp\in D\}$ and, for $t\in T_{x,p}$,
$\phi(t):=f(x+tp)$. Wherever $t$ is an interior point of $T_{x,p}$,
the chain rule gives
$\phi'(t)=\langle\nabla f(x+tp),p\rangle$, using the gradient convention
of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the Euclidean inner product of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. A direction is a **descent direction** at
$x$ when $\phi'(0)=\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle<0$.

Assume for the line-search conditions below that $p$ is a descent direction
at $x$.
Fix constants $0<c_1<c_2<1/2$. A feasible step $t>0$ is a **Wolfe step**
when
$$
\phi(t)\le\phi(0)+c_1t\phi'(0),\qquad \phi'(t)\ge c_2\phi'(0).
$$
It is a **strong Wolfe step** when it satisfies the first inequality and
$$
|\phi'(t)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|.
$$
The first inequality is the Armijo sufficient-decrease condition. The second
Wolfe inequality is the curvature condition. Every strong Wolfe step is a
Wolfe step, because $\phi'(0)<0$ and the strong curvature bound implies
$\phi'(t)\ge-c_2|\phi'(0)|=c_2\phi'(0)$.

For a descent direction define its **descent angle** $\theta\in[0,\pi/2)$ by
$$
\cos\theta:=-\frac{\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle}{\|\nabla f(x)\|_2\|p\|_2}.
$$
The denominator is nonzero for a descent direction. The Cauchy–Schwarz
inequality ensures $0<\cos\theta\le1$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:D\to\mathbb R$ be $C^1$,
let $x\in D$, and let $p\in\mathbb R^n$ satisfy
$\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle<0$. Fix $0<c_1<c_2<1/2$ and finite
budgets $E,Z\in\mathbb N$ for expansion and zoom trials. Use the functions
$\phi(t)=f(x+tp)$ and $\phi'(t)=\langle\nabla f(x+tp),p\rangle$ from
[[def-wolfe-and-strong-wolfe-conditions]]. **Output:** either a positive
strong Wolfe step, or one of `invalid-direction`, `domain-exit`, and
`evaluation-budget-exhausted`.

1. If $\langle\nabla f(x),p\rangle\ge0$, return `invalid-direction`.
   Set $a:=0$ and $t:=1$. For at most $E$ expansion trials, in order:
   - If $x+tp\notin D$, return `domain-exit` without evaluating the trial.
   - Evaluate $\phi(t)$ and $\phi'(t)$. If
     $\phi(t)>\phi(0)+c_1t\phi'(0)$ or $\phi(t)\ge\phi(a)$, call the zoom
     procedure below with the ordered endpoint pair $(a,t)$ and return its
     output.
   - If $|\phi'(t)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|$, return $t$ as a strong Wolfe step.
   - If $\phi'(t)\ge0$, call zoom with the reversed endpoint pair $(t,a)$ and
     return its output.
   - Otherwise set $a:=t$ and $t:=2t$.
2. If the expansion budget is exhausted, return `evaluation-budget-exhausted`.

For `zoom(a,b)`, preserve the endpoint order even when $b<a$. For at most
$Z$ zoom trials, in order:

1. Set $m:=(a+b)/2$. If $x+mp\notin D$, return `domain-exit` without
   evaluating the trial.
2. Evaluate $\phi(m)$ and $\phi'(m)$. If
   $\phi(m)>\phi(0)+c_1m\phi'(0)$ or $\phi(m)\ge\phi(a)$, set $b:=m$.
   Otherwise, if $|\phi'(m)|\le c_2|\phi'(0)|$, return $m$ as a strong Wolfe
   step. In the remaining branch, if $\phi'(m)(b-a)\ge0$, first set
   $b:=a$; then set $a:=m$.
3. If the zoom budget is exhausted, return `evaluation-budget-exhausted`.

The procedure returns a step only after both strong Wolfe inequalities have
been checked. Finite budgets and domain exits may return failure even when a
strong Wolfe step exists; no convergence claim follows from the procedure
alone.

Let $A$ be a square matrix over $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$ and let $b$ be a
vector of matching size. Define

$$K_0(A,b):=\{0\},$$

and for $m\ge 1$ define the $m$th **Krylov subspace**

$$K_m(A,b):=\operatorname{span}\{b,Ab,\dots,A^{m-1}b\}.$$

Thus $K_m(A,b)\subseteq K_{m+1}(A,b)$ for every $m\ge 0$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

derivations.claim:
By [F1], $\log$ is defined on $[1,x]$. If $x=1$, [F2] gives
$\log x=0$. If $x>1$, [F2] gives continuity of $\log$ on $[1,x]$, and
[F3] gives differentiability on $(1,x)$. By [F4],
there is $c\in(1,x)$ such that
$$\log x-\log1=\frac{x-1}{c},$$
so $\log x=(x-1)/c$.

In the $x=1$ case the claimed inequalities are equalities except
$x-1\le x$. In the $x>1$ case, $c>1$ and $x-1>0$, so
$0<(x-1)/c<x-1<x$. Combining with step 1.1 proves all three inequalities.
